rows.label: before-original-text
rows.textSynthesized: The ionosphere changes with the time of day and with solar activity. It delays lower frequencies more, in proportion to one over the frequency squared. A receiver listening on two frequencies can compare the delays and correct for it. With the newer civil signal L2C, civilian receivers can do that.

rows.textSynthesized: Relativity is not only for satellites. NIST physicists once ran two clocks just a foot apart in height, and they ticked at different rates. Gravity changes how time passes, and every time that blue dot appears, GPS has accounted for it.

rows.label: before-original-text
rows.textSynthesized: Between the satellite and your phone, the signal crosses the ionosphere and the troposphere, and both add delay. Dry air alone adds about two point three meters straight overhead, and about ten meters for satellites low on the horizon. Water vapor adds only tens of centimeters, but it changes quickly and is hard to model.
